notes.title: Scope & the LEGB Rule

headings.text: What does the B in LEGB refer to, and why does it matter that it's searched last?
Explain UnboundLocalError. Why does reading a name before assigning it in the same function fail, when reading a global of the same name would have worked?
A junior writes def make_handlers(): return [lambda: i for i in range(3)] and every handler returns 2. What's happening, and how do you fix it?
You're reviewing a config module that mutates module-level globals from inside functions using global, and it has started behaving flakily under a new thread pool. Redesign the scope discipline.

📚 Reference Links

  • Scopes & namespaces — Tutorial: Python scopes and namespaces

  • Naming and binding — Execution model: naming and binding

  • global — Reference: the global statement

  • nonlocal — Reference: the nonlocal statement

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Python scope and the LEGB rule

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

LEGB gets taught as four letters in an order, which makes it sound like a lookup rule and nothing more — and then the first time someone meets UnboundLocalError the rule appears to be violated, because the name they are reading is right there at module level and Python refuses to see it.

The problem it solves is a family of bugs that never raise at definition time: a counter that silently stops incrementing, a shadowed built-in that fails a thousand lines away, a loop of callbacks all wired to the last item. None of them look like scope bugs in a diff.

So carry this question through: when does Python decide which scope a name belongs to? The letters are the easy half. The timing is the half that produces the errors.

2. What Python normally does

Start with the thing that works so smoothly nobody thinks about it.

LIMIT = 10

def check(n):
    return n < LIMIT

You never declared LIMIT inside check, never imported it, never passed it. You just used it:

>>> check(3)
True

Python found it by searching outward. When it hits a bare name it has four namespaces to try, in a fixed order, and it stops at the first one that has it:

    reading a bare name inside check()

    L  Local        check's own names            n
        ↓ miss
    E  Enclosing    any enclosing function        (none here)
        ↓ miss
    G  Global       the module's namespace        LIMIT  ← found, stop
        ↓
    B  Built-in     the builtins namespace        len, range, print…
        ↓ miss
                    NameError

That is LEGB, and the "stop at the first hit" part is doing more work than it looks. It is why you can define a function called len and break every len() call in that module — your name is found at G before the interpreter ever reaches B. Built-ins are not privileged; they are just last.

The important half is that all of this applies to reading. Reading reaches outward as far as it needs to, and costs you nothing:

>>> def show():
...     return LIMIT        # no declaration required
...
>>> show()
10

So by default a name you only read is searched for outward through four namespaces, and the first match wins.

3. What changes

Now add an assignment. One line, at the end, after the read.

LIMIT = 10

def check(n):
    result = n < LIMIT      # unchanged
    LIMIT = 99              # new line, AFTER the read
    return result

>>> check(3)
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'LIMIT' where it is not
associated with a value

Look at where that error is. It is on the first line — the one that worked a moment ago and has not been edited. Adding an assignment three lines below changed the meaning of a line above it.

That is the rule people miss. Assignment anywhere in a function body makes the name local for the entire body, including every line before the assignment. The decision is made once, by scanning the whole function, before any of it runs. So the read no longer goes looking outward at all — it goes straight to a local slot, finds it empty, and raises.

READ ONLY                        ASSIGNED ANYWHERE IN THE BODY

check's names: n                 check's names: n, result, LIMIT
                                                          ▲
  LIMIT ──┐                                        classified local
          │  searches outward                      for the WHOLE body
          ▼
    L → E → G ✓  found at module            LIMIT ──→ local slot (empty)
                                                         ▼
                                                   UnboundLocalError
                                                   (never looks outward)

And note what counts as an assignment, because the list is wider than =: LIMIT += 1, for LIMIT in …, import LIMIT, def LIMIT, with … as LIMIT, except … as LIMIT, and the walrus. Any of them classifies the name.

The escape hatches exist precisely because of this. global LIMIT says assignment in here should rebind the module-level name, not make a local; nonlocal LIMIT says the same for the nearest enclosing function scope:

def check(n):
    global LIMIT
    result = n < LIMIT      # reads the module-level one again
    LIMIT = 99              # rebinds the module-level one
    return result

The trade in one sentence: Python gives you fast, statically-known locals and no variable declarations, and you pay by having assignment silently declare — for the whole function, retroactively.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, Python searches four namespaces. In CPython, only two of the four are ever searched at runtime, because the compiler has already decided which bucket each name is in — and that is the fact the whole topic rests on.

When a function is compiled, the compiler walks the entire body once and sorts every name into a category, which it bakes into the code object:

  • local → listed in co_varnames, compiled to LOAD_FAST / STORE_FAST, a direct index into the frame's array of slots. No dictionary, no search.

  • cell or free → co_cellvars (I own this, an inner function captures it) and co_freevars (I capture this from an enclosing function), compiled to LOAD_DEREF. This is the E of LEGB, and it is the closure machinery.

  • global or builtin → compiled to LOAD_GLOBAL, which checks the module dict and then the builtins dict at runtime.

Read the branches and three things that felt like separate rules turn out to be one.

UnboundLocalError and NameError are different errors because they come from different opcodes. An unbound local is a LOAD_FAST against an empty slot — the interpreter knows the name is local and knows it has no value, so there is nothing to fall back to. A NameError is LOAD_GLOBAL missing in both dicts. Naming the right one in an interview is a quick signal that you know the classification happened at compile time.

The L in LEGB is not a dictionary. Locals live in a fixed-size array indexed by number, which is why local access is meaningfully faster than global access and why the "bind it to a local before the hot loop" trick works at all. G and B genuinely are dictionary lookups.

global and nonlocal are compiler directives, not runtime operations. They do not execute; they change which opcode the compiler emits for that name. That is why nonlocal x with no enclosing binding is a SyntaxError at compile time rather than an error when the line runs — there is no opcode the compiler could emit.

One boundary worth knowing because it surprises people: class bodies do not participate in the E of LEGB. A class body executes in its own namespace, but methods defined inside it do not close over it, so a method referencing a class-level name directly gets a NameError rather than finding it in an enclosing scope. It has to go through self or the class name.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
_pool = None                          # module-level singleton

def get_pool():
    global _pool                      # without this, the assignment below makes
    if _pool is None:                 # _pool local and the read raises
        _pool = create_pool()
    return _pool                      # ✅ legitimate `global`: single writer,
                                      #    initialised once, never mutated after

def make_rate_limiter(limit: int):
    used = 0                          # lives in a cell (co_cellvars)

    def allow() -> bool:
        nonlocal used                 # rebind the ENCLOSING `used`, not a new local
        if used >= limit:             # `limit` is read-only → free var, no declaration
            return False
        used += 1
        return True

    return allow                      # the closure carries `used` and `limit`

Two different tools that look similar and are not. global reaches all the way out to the module namespace and is only defensible here because there is a single writer initialising a singleton once. nonlocal reaches exactly one level out, into a scope that is private to this closure — which is why make_rate_limiter is safe to call a hundred times and get a hundred independent counters, while get_pool is process-wide shared state and would need a lock the moment two threads could race it.

Note the asymmetry in allow: limit needs no declaration because it is only read, while used needs nonlocal because it is assigned. That is Section 3's rule, doing its job.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It prints the compiler's classification of two nearly identical functions before either of them runs, which turns the whole topic from a runtime mystery into something you can read off the code object.

x = "module-level"

def reads_only():
    return x

def reads_then_assigns():
    y = x                  # identical line
    x = "local"            # ...but this exists
    return y

print(reads_only.__code__.co_varnames)          # ?
print(reads_then_assigns.__code__.co_varnames)  # ?
print(reads_only())                             # ?
print(reads_then_assigns())                     # ?

# what to look for: 'x' appears in the second function's co_varnames, and that
#                   alone decides which one raises — no line ever ran
# naive model would predict: both read the module-level x, since the assignment
#                   comes after the read

The first prints (). The second prints ('y', 'x'). Then reads_only() returns "module-level" and reads_then_assigns() raises UnboundLocalError.

What that proves is that the decision is a property of the compiled function, not of execution order. co_varnames was populated when def executed — you inspected it before calling anything — and the two functions were routed to different opcodes on that basis. This is also the fastest way to debug a real UnboundLocalError in unfamiliar code: print co_varnames and the name will be sitting in it, which tells you to go hunting for the assignment you did not notice.

7. The deeper mental model

Zoom out and this is the same split you have already met in default arguments, wearing different clothes:

      COMPILE TIME                        RUNTIME
   (once, when def executes)          (every call)

   which scope each name              what value is in the slot
   belongs to                              ↓
        ↓                              LOAD_FAST  → frame array
   co_varnames  (local)                LOAD_DEREF → closure cell
   co_cellvars  (I'm captured)         LOAD_GLOBAL→ module dict, then builtins
   co_freevars  (I capture)
   global / nonlocal directives

Python has no variable declarations, so it needed some other way to know a name's scope without running the code — and the answer it picked was to treat assignment as the declaration, retroactively, across the whole function. Every confusing thing in this note follows from that one decision: the error on the line before the assignment, the fact that for and import count, the need for global and nonlocal as compile-time overrides.

That is also the trade the language made on purpose. Because scope is static, locals can be array slots instead of dictionary keys, which is the single biggest reason function-local code is as fast as it is. A language where scope were decided line by line at runtime would need a dictionary lookup for every name, every time.

So the honest one-line summary is not "Python searches four namespaces". It is that Python decides a name's scope by scanning, not by executing — and LEGB is only the order it searches once the scanning has already routed the name.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
LEGB, in resolution order? Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in. First match wins; the search stops there.
When is a name classified local? At compile time, if it is assigned anywhere in the body — including after the read.
UnboundLocalError vs NameError? Empty local slot (LOAD_FAST) vs not found in module or builtins (LOAD_GLOBAL).
What does global x do? Compiler directive: assignment rebinds the module-level x instead of creating a local.
What does nonlocal x do? Same, but targets the nearest enclosing function scope. Cannot reach module scope.
What counts as an assignment? =, +=, for targets, import, def, class, with…as, except…as, walrus.
The late-binding closure trap? Closures capture the cell, read at call time — [lambda: i for i in range(3)] all give 2.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the classification-then-lookup split is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes A–J and reconstruct it cold; the answer key is the compile-time "assigned anywhere?" branch routing to LOAD_FAST / LOAD_DEREF / LOAD_GLOBAL, with two distinct error exits.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What does the B in LEGB refer to, and why does it matter that it's searched last?

The B is Built-in — the builtins namespace holding len, range, print, Exception and the rest. It is searched last, which is exactly why you can shadow a built-in: assigning list = [1, 2] creates a name found at Local or Global, and every later list(...) in that scope raises TypeError: 'list' object is not callable.

The useful framing is that built-ins are not magic — builtins is an ordinary, introspectable, shadowable module. That makes it a real footgun with names like id, type, input and sum, and occasionally a deliberate technique, as when a test patches open. A name you define always beats the interpreter's default of the same name.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Explain UnboundLocalError. Why does reading a name before assigning it in the same function fail, when reading a global of the same name would have worked?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know scope is resolved statically at compile time rather than dynamically, line by line.

When CPython compiles a function it scans the entire body first and classifies every name. Any name that is the target of an assignment anywhere in that body — =, augmented assignment, a for target, import, def, with ... as, the walrus — becomes local for the whole function. It goes into co_varnames and every reference compiles to LOAD_FAST, a direct index into the frame's slot array rather than a namespace lookup. All of this is finished before a single line executes; you can print co_varnames and see it.

So x = x + 1 where x is otherwise a global fails on the right-hand side: the assignment made x local everywhere, LOAD_FAST finds the slot empty, and there is no fallback, because the interpreter is not searching — it already knows where the name lives. x += 1 fails identically, since augmented assignment is still an assignment. That also explains why this is a different exception from NameError: NameError comes from LOAD_GLOBAL missing in both the module dict and builtins, whereas UnboundLocalError means the name was correctly resolved to a local that has not been stored yet. The fix is global x or nonlocal x, which are compiler directives that change which opcode is emitted.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A junior writes def make_handlers(): return [lambda: i for i in range(3)] and every handler returns 2. What's happening, and how do you fix it?

📍 Seen in the wild: shows up constantly with event handlers, retry callbacks, and building partially-applied functions in a loop.

This is late binding, and it is the same mechanism seen from the enclosing side. Each lambda captures the variable i, not its value — concretely, all three close over one shared cell. The comprehension runs to completion leaving i == 2, and because the lambdas read the cell lazily when they are called rather than when they are created, all three see 2. Nothing in Python captures by value; closures capture bindings.

The canonical fix is a per-iteration default argument, [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)], which works because default arguments are evaluated eagerly at definition time and stored in __defaults__ — so each lambda snapshots the current value into its own parameter. The alternative is a factory, def make(i): return lambda: i, called once per iteration, which creates a genuinely fresh enclosing scope and therefore a fresh cell each time. functools.partial(fn, i) does the same job by binding the argument immediately.

The reason it is worth knowing both fixes is that they fail differently under review. The default-argument form adds a parameter to the callable's public signature, which matters if something else inspects or calls it with positional arguments; the factory form costs an extra function but leaves the signature clean.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

You're reviewing a config module that mutates module-level globals from inside functions using global, and it has started behaving flakily under a new thread pool. Redesign the scope discipline.

🎯 Really testing: whether you recognise module globals as unsynchronised shared mutable state, and can eliminate a concurrency bug class by scoping rather than by locking.

The binding constraint is that global-mutated module state is process-wide shared mutable state with no synchronisation. Under a thread pool two workers racing on the same global produce torn reads and lost updates, and the flakiness is the signature — non-deterministic values that correlate with concurrency rather than with input. What makes it hard to spot in review is that global x sits at the top of a function and reads like a local declaration, so the mutation three lines down looks scoped when it is anything but.

The first move is to stop treating the module namespace as a mutable store. I would replace the globals with an explicit object threaded through call arguments — a frozen dataclass Config constructed once at startup and injected — so that every function reads immutable state it was handed, and nothing reaches up into module scope to write. That converts an invisible dependency into a parameter, which has the secondary benefit of making the module testable without monkeypatching.

Where per-task mutable state is genuinely required, that goes in a contextvars.ContextVar rather than a global. This is the specific detail worth stating, because threading.local solves it only for threads and breaks under asyncio, where many tasks share one thread — ContextVar is correct for both, which is why it is what the frameworks moved to for request-scoped state. global would survive only for true constants bound once at import and never rebound.

The failure mode I would monitor first is one request's response reflecting another request's parameters — the read-your-neighbour's-writes signature. A concurrency test that fires two requests with deliberately different config and asserts the responses do not cross is cheap, and it fails loudly on exactly this bug while a sequential test suite cannot see it at all.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Read an outer name Rebind an outer name Assignment creates a local? Failure if no binding exists
(default) ✅ LEGB search works ❌ makes it local instead ✅ yes NameError at runtime
global x reads module scope ✅ rebinds module-level x ❌ writes go to the module creates it on assignment
nonlocal x reads enclosing function ✅ rebinds nearest enclosing x ❌ writes go to that scope SyntaxError at compile time

nonlocal requires the name to already exist in an enclosing function scope — it cannot reach module scope, and it is rejected at compile time rather than at runtime if no binding is found.

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how scope resolves, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Python decides whether a name is local when it reaches the assignment line at runtime."

✅ Reality: Locality is decided at compile time by scanning the whole function. An assignment anywhere makes the name local everywhere in that function, including lines above it. Section 6 shows this in co_varnames before anything runs.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Closures in a loop capture the current value of the loop variable."

✅ Reality: They capture the variable — a shared cell — and read it when called. Every closure sees the final value unless you snapshot it with a default argument, a factory, or partial.

❌ Misconception: "If the local isn't set yet, Python falls back to the global."

✅ Reality: It never falls back. LOAD_FAST against an empty slot raises UnboundLocalError — the interpreter already knows the name is local and has nowhere else to look.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Scope resolution gets conflated with the late-binding closure trap, and they are two views of one mechanism rather than one problem. LEGB explains where a name is found; closures explain when the value is read. The loop bug is not a resolution-order failure — resolution correctly finds the enclosing variable — the surprise is that the read is deferred to call time, so it observes the final binding. Separately, do not confuse reading an outer name, which needs no declaration at all, with rebinding one, which is the only thing global and nonlocal are for.

Interview Traps

  • Saying "it looks it up globally if the local isn't set yet" — the exact inverse. Naming UnboundLocalError and saying it never falls back is what signals you understand compile-time classification.

  • Giving the loop-closure fix as "add i=i" with no reason — the reason is that default arguments are evaluated eagerly at definition time, so i=i snapshots the value. Without that, it reads as a memorised incantation.

  • Confusing nonlocal with global — nonlocal targets the nearest enclosing function, global targets the module, and claiming nonlocal can reach module scope is an instant tell.

  • Forgetting that for, import, def and with…as are assignments — any of them classifies a name local and can trigger the error, and this is the follow-up that catches people who only memorised the = case.

  • Reciting the four letters and stopping — LEGB as an ordering is junior-level recall. The senior answer is the compile-time classification that happens before the ordering is ever consulted.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • global for a module-level singleton initialised once — a lazily-built connection pool or a memoised module cache, where there is a single writer and the value is never mutated afterwards.

  • nonlocal for a genuinely stateful closure — a counter, accumulator or rate limiter whose state is private to that closure and not visible to anything else. This is the functional alternative to a one-attribute class.

  • Plain LEGB read-through for constants and helpers — reading a module-level name needs no declaration, and adding global when you are only reading is noise that misleads the next reader into thinking something is mutated.

  • contextvars.ContextVar instead of global whenever the value must be isolated per thread or per asyncio task — this is the one that matters, because threading.local silently does the wrong thing under asyncio.

  • Binding a global to a local before a hot loop — _len = len is a real optimisation, because LOAD_FAST beats LOAD_GLOBAL. Reach for it only with a profile in hand.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't use global to pass data between functions — it is hidden coupling and shared mutable state, invisible at the call site, and a race the moment anything is concurrent. Pass an argument or return a value.

  • Don't shadow built-ins — list, dict, id, type, input, sum and filter are the usual casualties, and the resulting TypeError surfaces far from the assignment that caused it.

  • Don't rely on late binding when building callables in a loop — always snapshot, with a default argument, a factory, or functools.partial.

  • Don't expect nonlocal to reach module scope — there is no enclosing function binding to find, so it is a SyntaxError. Use global, or restructure so the state is passed.

  • Don't reach for a closure once the captured state grows past two or three variables — at that point a small class with attributes is more readable and far easier to debug, because the state has names you can inspect rather than cells you cannot.

🔖 Version discipline

LEGB, global and nonlocal semantics are stable across all of Python 3.x. Two nuances worth stating against a version: comprehensions and generator expressions have had their own scope since Python 3, so the loop variable does not leak — but the late-binding trap still applies inside them, because the closures share that comprehension-internal cell. contextvars is 3.7+. The exact wording of UnboundLocalError changed in 3.11 to the friendlier "cannot access local variable … where it is not associated with a value", so do not quote the old message as current.

13. Production Reality

Scope bugs are silent correctness bugs rather than crashes, which is what makes a semantic rule worth a CORE note.

Why It Matters in Production

None of the three classic failures announce themselves at definition time. An accidental global-mutated counter becomes a race the day the service gets a thread pool. A shadowed built-in produces a TypeError a thousand lines from the assignment that caused it, in a function that looks blameless. A late-binding closure in a loop wires every retry callback to the last URL, so the retry logic "works" in a test with one item and silently retries the wrong endpoint in production.

The business framing is that these all survive review and single-call unit tests, and they surface as intermittent wrong behaviour rather than as errors — which puts them in the expensive category where the investigation starts in the wrong place. Knowing that scope is resolved statically, and that closures capture bindings rather than values, is what lets you catch all three by reading a diff.

Real World Usage

Not applicable — this is a language-level resolution rule rather than a distinguishing production feature. Its practical footprints are everywhere, though: the migration of request-scoped state from module globals to contextvars across web and async frameworks, the default-argument snapshot idiom in any codebase that builds callbacks in loops, and the _local_name = global_name hoisting that shows up in hot loops in the standard library itself.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — LEGB is a semantic resolution rule with no defensible citable benchmark, and per the no-fabrication rule no numbers beat invented ones. The one performance-adjacent fact is directional and worth stating as such: LOAD_FAST is an array index while LOAD_GLOBAL is a dict lookup with a builtins fallback, which is the basis of the hoist-to-local trick — measure it in your own profile rather than quoting a ratio.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Local reads are array-slot access and beat global dict lookups; the gap only matters inside hot loops.
💰 Memory Closures keep their enclosing cells alive for the closure's lifetime, so a captured large object is not collected until the closure dies.
🧮 CPU Negligible — resolution is compile-time classification plus an array or dict access.
📈 Scale global mutable state becomes a correctness bottleneck under concurrency long before it becomes a performance one.
🔧 Maintainability global and nonlocal hide where state lives; explicit passing makes data flow reviewable.
🐍 CPython-specific Name categories are baked into the code object (co_varnames, co_cellvars, co_freevars) at compile time and are directly inspectable.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Names, binding and assignment — LEGB decides which binding a name refers to; that note covers what a binding is.

  • The CPython execution model — the compile-then-execute split this whole topic depends on.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • First-class functions and closures — cells and free variables are the E of LEGB, seen from the inside.

  • Decorators — a decorator is a closure over the wrapped function, so its state lives in exactly this machinery.

  • contextvars — the correct per-task replacement for mutable module globals.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Explicit argument passing and dependency injection — when global would create hidden coupling.

  • A small class with instance attributes — when a closure's captured state grows past one or two variables.

  • functools.partial — freezing a value at creation time without a default-argument parameter.

🧩 Composes with

  • The shared-default trap — the default-argument loop fix works because defaults are evaluated at definition time, which is that note's rule.

  • Comprehension scope — why the loop variable does not leak while the closure still late-binds.

15. Lock it in

Reading searches outward: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in, first hit wins.
Assigning declares — at compile time, for the whole function, retroactively.

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 Check your desk, then the team room, then the building directory, then the dictionary in the lobby.

You need the meaning of a name. You check your own desk first, then your team's room, then the building directory, and finally the dictionary bolted to the lobby wall — stopping the instant you find it. But if you wrote that name on your own desk at any point today, you refuse to look past your desk at all, even when the slot is still empty.

Stopping at the first hit is resolution short-circuiting. "Wrote it on your desk at any point today" is assignment anywhere in the body classifying the name local at compile time. And the empty desk slot you refuse to look past is UnboundLocalError — the name resolved correctly, to a place with nothing in it yet.

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Closures get described as "a function that remembers its environment", which sounds like the function took a copy of something on its way out. It did not, and almost every closure bug people actually hit comes from believing that it did.

The problem it solves is real and everywhere: you want a function pre-configured with some data — a validator that knows its schema, a retry wrapper that knows its limit, a callback that knows which row it belongs to — without building a class for every one of them.

So hold this question the whole way: when the enclosing function returns, where does its local variable go? The answer turns out to be neither "it dies" nor "it was copied", and that third option is the entire topic.

2. What Python normally does

Two ordinary facts first, because the interesting behaviour is what happens when they collide.

The first is that functions are objects like anything else. def builds an object and binds a name to it, and you can do anything with that object you could do with a list:

def shout(s):
    return s.upper()

handlers = {"loud": shout}          # store it
f = shout                           # bind another name
print(f.__name__, f("hi"))          # introspect it, call it

shout HI

The second is that a function call's locals do not survive the call. Calling a function builds a frame to hold them, and returning throws the frame away:

def outer():
    msg = "hello"
    return len(msg)

Once outer() returns, msg is gone — nothing references it, its refcount drops to zero, and it is freed. That is the normal lifecycle, and it is why functions do not leak memory by default.

Now nest a function inside, but have the inner one use only its own names:

def outer():
    msg = "hello"
    def inner():
        return "standalone"
    return inner

fn = outer()

>>> fn.__closure__
None

__closure__ is None. inner is a perfectly good first-class function that happened to be defined inside another one, and nothing was captured — because nothing needed to be. msg died with the frame exactly as before.

    outer() called          outer() returns

    ┌─ frame ─────┐
    │ msg → "hello"│   ──→   frame discarded
    │ inner → fn   │         "hello" freed
    └──────────────┘         fn survives, carrying nothing

So by default a function is just an object, and the frame that created it is discarded the moment it returns.

3. What changes

Change one thing. Have the inner function read the enclosing variable.

def outer():
    msg = "hello"
    def inner():
        return msg              # the only difference
    return inner

fn = outer()

outer has returned. Its frame is gone. And yet:

>>> fn()
'hello'

Something kept msg alive, and it is visible on the function object:

>>> fn.__closure__
(<cell at 0x7f2a1c0b4d00: str object at 0x7f2a1c1e2530>,)
>>> fn.__closure__[0].cell_contents
'hello'
>>> fn.__code__.co_freevars
('msg',)

That is a cell — a one-slot heap object holding a pointer to the value. Because inner referenced msg, the compiler stopped storing msg as a plain frame local and stored it in a cell instead, and the returned function holds a reference to that cell. The frame died; the cell did not, because something still points at it.

NO CAPTURE                      CAPTURE

outer frame                     outer frame
 msg → "hello"  ──✗ freed        msg ──┐
                                        ├──→ ┌─ cell ──────┐
fn.__closure__ = None            (frame  │    │ → "hello"   │
                                  dies)  │    └─────────────┘
                                         │          ▲
                                 fn.__closure__ = (cell,)

And here is the part that matters more than the survival: the cell is shared and live, not a snapshot. Two inner functions from the same call get the same cell, and a write through one is visible through the other:

def outer():
    n = 0
    def bump():
        nonlocal n              # write through the cell
        n += 1
    def get():
        return n                # read the same cell
    return bump, get

bump, get = outer()
bump(); bump()

>>> get()
2

Note the nonlocal. Reading a free variable needs no declaration, but assigning one would make it a new local by the ordinary scoping rule — nonlocal is what tells the compiler to write through the cell instead.

The trade in one sentence: you get functions that carry live private state with no class and no boilerplate, and you pay by keeping everything in those cells alive for as long as the function object lives, and by reading the value at call time rather than at creation time.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Conceptually, the inner function "remembers its environment". In CPython the mechanism is narrow and fully inspectable: one extra level of indirection, decided at compile time.

When the compiler sees an inner function referencing a name from an enclosing function, it reclassifies that name in both scopes. In the enclosing function it becomes a cell variable, listed in co_cellvars, so the frame stores a cell rather than the value directly. In the inner function it becomes a free variable, listed in co_freevars, compiled to LOAD_DEREF and STORE_DEREF rather than LOAD_FAST.

Three consequences fall out of that one indirection, and they are the three things interviewers probe.

Capture is by reference, because there is no copy anywhere in the diagram. The cell holds a pointer, the closure holds the cell, and the read happens when the closure runs. That is simultaneously the feature — sibling closures sharing state, decorators carrying configuration — and the late-binding trap, which is the same fact observed by someone who wanted a snapshot.

Lifetime follows the closure, not the call. The cell is kept alive by an ordinary reference from __closure__, so everything reachable from the captured value stays alive as long as the function object does. Capture a request object or a database handle in a closure you store in a registry, and you have pinned it for the process lifetime. This is a genuine leak vector and it does not look like one.

One cell per enclosing call, not per function. Each call to the enclosing function builds a fresh frame and therefore a fresh cell, which is exactly why a factory gives you independent state per call while a loop inside one call does not. Section 6 shows both halves of that in one paste.

Worth naming precisely: a nested function is only a closure if it has free variables. If __closure__ is None, you have a nested function and nothing more — being returned or passed around does not make something a closure, capturing does.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
def make_counter(start: int = 0):
    count = start                      # becomes a cellvar: inner fns reference it

    def increment(step: int = 1) -> int:
        nonlocal count                 # ✅ write through the cell, not a new local
        count += step
        return count

    def value() -> int:
        return count                   # reads the SAME cell, live

    return increment, value            # two closures, one shared cell

inc, val = make_counter(10)
inc(); inc(5)
print(val())                                   # 16 — val sees inc's writes
print(inc.__closure__[0].cell_contents)        # 16 — the cell itself
print(inc.__code__.co_freevars)                # ('count',)

The two returned functions are the point. They were compiled separately, they have different names and different signatures, and they share one piece of mutable state that nothing outside can reach — no attribute to poke, no dictionary to corrupt. That is the thing a closure gives you that a class does not: state that is genuinely private rather than private by convention.

It is also the thing to be suspicious of. The moment you find yourself returning a third closure to reset the counter, you have built a class with worse ergonomics and no introspection, and should write the class.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It makes two independent counters and then compares the cell objects directly, which settles both halves of the sharing question at once.

def make():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    def get():
        return n
    return inc, get

a_inc, a_get = make()
b_inc, b_get = make()
a_inc(); a_inc()

print(a_get(), b_get())                                  # ?
print(a_inc.__closure__[0] is a_get.__closure__[0])      # ?
print(a_inc.__closure__[0] is b_inc.__closure__[0])      # ?

# what to look for: siblings from ONE call share a cell; the same function from a
#                   SECOND call gets a different one
# naive model would predict: either all four share state, or none of them do

You get 2 0, then True, then False.

That is the whole lifetime rule, demonstrated rather than asserted. a_inc and a_get came out of the same call, so they hold the identical cell object and see each other's writes. b_inc came out of a second call, which built a second frame and therefore a second cell, so it starts at zero and can never be affected by a_inc. Sharing is scoped to the enclosing call, which is why a factory function is the reliable fix for the loop-capture bug: each iteration that calls the factory gets its own frame, and therefore its own cell.

7. The deeper mental model

Zoom out and the cell stops being a closure detail and becomes an instance of something more general:

    NORMAL CALL                    SOMETHING OUTLIVES IT

    frame created                  frame created
        ↓                              ↓
    locals in slots                locals promoted to cells
        ↓                              ↓
    return                         return — frame discarded
        ↓                              ↓
    frame discarded                cells survive, held by
    everything freed               whatever still points at them

Python keeps producing variations on the right-hand column, and they are all the same idea: some piece of a function call needs to outlive the call, so the runtime stops treating it as stack-shaped. A closure keeps the bindings alive in cells. A generator keeps the entire frame alive, instruction pointer and all, so it can be resumed. A coroutine is that same suspended frame with a scheduler driving it. Even a traceback is a frame that outlived its call, retained so you can inspect it.

Seen that way, "first-class functions" and "closures" are two halves of one capability rather than two topics. Functions being objects is what lets one escape the scope it was defined in; cells are what make that escape meaningful, by letting it take its context along. Without the first you could not return inner; without the second, returning it would be pointless.

So the honest one-line summary is not "closures remember their environment". It is that a closure is a function plus the cells it kept alive — and every surprising thing about closures is a consequence of those cells being shared, live, and refcounted like any other object.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes a function "first-class"? It is an object — assign it, pass it, return it, store it in a data structure.
What is a closure, precisely? An inner function with free variables, carrying the live cells that hold them.
Nested function vs closure? __closure__ is None vs a tuple of cells. Being returned doesn't make it a closure.
Where is the captured value stored? A cell object's cell_contents; names listed in __code__.co_freevars.
Capture by value or reference? By reference — a shared cell, read at call time, so later writes are visible.
How do you write to a captured variable? nonlocal. Plain assignment would create a new local instead.
One cell per what? Per enclosing call — which is why a factory isolates state and a loop does not.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the cell surviving the frame is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes A–H and reconstruct cold; the answer key is compile-time reclassification → cell allocated → attached to __closure__ → frame discarded → cell survives → LOAD_DEREF reads it live.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between a nested function and a closure?

Every closure is a nested function, but not every nested function is a closure. A nested function becomes one only when it references a free variable — a name bound in an enclosing function scope — so that the binding has to outlive the enclosing call.

You can check it directly rather than reasoning about it: inner.__closure__ is None for a self-contained inner function, and a tuple of cell objects when it captures anything, with the captured names listed in inner.__code__.co_freevars. That tuple is the concrete signature of a closure. Being returned or passed around is not — that is just being first-class.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through what CPython builds when a function captures an enclosing variable. What is a cell?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand closures as shared mutable cells rather than as copied values.

When the compiler sees an inner function referencing a name from an enclosing function, it changes how that name is stored in both scopes. In the enclosing function the name becomes a cell variable (co_cellvars) rather than an ordinary local, so the frame holds a cell instead of the value. In the inner function it becomes a free variable (co_freevars), and every reference compiles to LOAD_DEREF rather than LOAD_FAST. A cell is a tiny heap object with a single slot, cell_contents, holding a pointer to the actual value, and both functions reach the value through it.

That indirection is the whole mechanism. Normally the enclosing frame is discarded on return, but the cell is kept alive by an ordinary reference from the returned function's __closure__ tuple — so the binding outlives the call by the same refcounting that keeps any other object alive. Because it is one shared cell, two closures created in the same enclosing call see each other's writes, and every read happens at call time rather than at definition time. That is why capture is by reference: nothing is copied, there is just a shared one-slot box. And it is why writing to a free variable needs nonlocal — without it, the assignment would follow the ordinary rule and create a new local instead of a cell write.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A colleague builds a list of callbacks in a loop, each meant to remember its index, but they all fire with the last index. Diagnose it and give two fixes.

📍 Seen in the wild: the single most common closure bug — event handlers, retry callbacks, and partially-applied functions built in a loop.

This is late binding, and it is the by-reference rule seen by someone who expected a snapshot. Every callback created in the loop captures the same cell, because the loop body runs inside one enclosing call and therefore has one frame and one binding for the loop variable. The closures read that cell lazily when invoked, and by then the loop has finished, so all of them see the final value. Nothing was copied incorrectly — nothing was copied at all.

The first fix is a default-argument snapshot, lambda i=i: ..., which works because default arguments are evaluated eagerly at definition time and stored in __defaults__, sidestepping the cell entirely. The second is a factory — def make_cb(i): return lambda: i, called once per iteration — which creates a genuinely new enclosing frame and therefore a new cell per callback. functools.partial(fn, i) achieves the same eager binding a third way.

They are not interchangeable in review, which is worth saying unprompted. The default-argument form adds a parameter to the callable's public signature, so anything that inspects it or calls it positionally can be surprised; the factory costs an extra function but leaves the signature clean and reads better once the body is more than one line. I would use the default argument for a throwaway lambda and the factory for anything a colleague has to maintain.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a rate limiter as a closure-based factory that many parts of a service can create independently, and tell me where the closure approach breaks versus a class.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know when a closure's private state is an asset and when it becomes a liability at scale.

The binding constraint is per-caller isolation: each make_limiter(rate) call must produce an independent limiter with its own token count, and closures give that for free, because each call creates a fresh frame and therefore fresh cells. I would return an allow() that reads and updates the token count through nonlocal, closing over rate, tokens and last_refill. For small single-method state this is genuinely better than a class — the state is unreachable from outside, so it cannot be corrupted by anything except the function that owns it.

The approach breaks when the interface grows. A closure exposes exactly one callable, so the moment you need reset(), current_tokens() for a metrics endpoint, or any introspection at all, you are either bolting attributes onto a function object or returning a tuple of cell-sharing closures — at which point a class with named methods is clearer, testable, and debuggable. Two harder limits matter at service scale: closures cannot be pickled, so they cannot cross a multiprocessing boundary or go into a task queue, and their captured state is invisible in a debugger and in logs, showing up as opaque cells rather than named attributes. So the rule I would state is: closure for one-method private state at the edges, class the instant it needs multiple methods, serialisation, or observability.

There is also a correctness caveat I would raise before anyone deploys it. A closure-based limiter is not thread-safe — tokens -= 1 is a read-modify-write through a cell with no lock, so under a thread pool two callers can both pass the check. That needs a threading.Lock captured in the same closure, or an asyncio primitive if the service is async, and it is the kind of thing the elegance of the closure form tends to hide.

The failure mode I would monitor first is unbounded growth from calling the factory per request rather than per client key. Each closure pins its cells, so a limiter created per request is a slow leak of cell objects that presents as gradual RSS growth tracking request volume rather than client count.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Closure Class instance
State lives in shared cell objects (__closure__) instance __dict__ or __slots__
Interface one callable, or a tuple of them many named methods
Best for single-method private state multi-method, evolving state
Privacy genuinely unreachable from outside private by convention only
Picklable? ❌ no — can't cross a process boundary ✅ yes, if the attributes are
Introspection / debugging poor — opaque cells good — named attributes
Write to state needs nonlocal plain self.x = ...
Isolation unit one enclosing call one instance

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how capture works, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A closure copies the enclosing variables into the inner function."

✅ Reality: It shares a live cell. The closure reads the current value at call time and sees any later write to the enclosing binding — which is the whole explanation for the loop trap.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "You can just assign to an enclosing variable inside the inner function to update it."

✅ Reality: Plain assignment creates a new local, and usually raises UnboundLocalError on the read. You need nonlocal for the compiler to emit a cell write.

❌ Misconception: "Returning a function from a function makes it a closure."

✅ Reality: Only capturing a free variable does. A returned inner function that uses no enclosing names has __closure__ is None — it is first-class, not a closure.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Closures get conflated with first-class functions, and the distinction is exactly the thing being tested. Being first-class — passable, returnable, storable — is necessary but not sufficient; a function is a closure only when it carries cells for free variables. Separately, do not conflate a closure with a generator: both let a function's state outlive a call, but a closure keeps only the captured bindings while a generator keeps the whole suspended frame, including where it was up to.

Interview Traps

  • Saying closures "capture values" — they capture variables, via cells. The by-value framing gets the loop question wrong and cannot explain sibling closures sharing state.

  • Forgetting nonlocal while whiteboarding a counter — count += 1 without it raises UnboundLocalError, and missing it signals you have not actually written stateful closures.

  • Describing the behaviour without naming cells — __closure__, cell_contents, co_freevars are what move the answer from "I've seen this" to "I know how it works".

  • Claiming closures can be sent to a process pool — they cannot be pickled, and this specific mistake sinks answers in concurrency design questions.

  • Not mentioning the lifetime consequence — that captured objects stay alive for the closure's lifetime is the production-relevant half, and leaving it out makes the answer academic.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Single-method private state at the edges — a counter, accumulator, memoiser or configured callback, where a class would be pure boilerplate and the state genuinely should not be reachable.

  • Factory functions that pre-configure behaviour — make_validator(schema), make_retry(max_attempts) — capturing configuration so the caller receives a ready-to-use function with a clean signature.

  • Inside decorators — the wrapper is a closure over the decorated function and over any decorator arguments; this is the single most common real use.

  • Per-iteration factories when building callables in a loop — the reliable way to give each callback its own cell rather than sharing one.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't use a closure once the state needs multiple methods — the moment you want reset() alongside increment(), a tuple of cell-sharing closures is harder to read, test and debug than a small class.

  • Don't capture large or expensive objects casually — a closure over a whole request, a response body, or a DB handle pins it for the closure's lifetime, and if the closure lands in a module-level registry that is the process lifetime.

  • Don't try to send closures across processes — pickle cannot serialise them or lambdas, so multiprocessing, concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor and most task queues will reject them. Use a top-level function, or functools.partial over one.

  • Don't rely on late binding in loops — snapshot with a default argument, a factory, or partial. A bare lambda: i captures the shared cell and every copy sees the final value.

  • Don't assume closure state is thread-safe — n += 1 through a cell is a read-modify-write with no lock, and the concise syntax hides that as effectively as a global does.

🔖 Version discipline

Closure and cell semantics are stable across all of Python 3.x, and __closure__, cell_contents, co_freevars and co_cellvars are long-standing CPython-observable attributes. nonlocal is Python 3.0+ and is the only way to rebind a free variable — material that shows mutable-container workarounds (count = [0]) is working around a Python 2 limitation and should not be copied. cell objects gained a writable cell_contents and a public constructor in 3.7, which matters only if you are constructing them by hand. Nothing here is affected by the specialising interpreter changes in 3.11–3.13, but the opcode names around LOAD_DEREF have moved, so disassemble on your own build before quoting bytecode.

13. Production Reality

Closures are the substrate under decorators, callbacks, deferred work and lightweight stateful helpers, which makes their failure modes unusually widely distributed.

Why It Matters in Production

Three distinct incidents trace back to this one mechanism. A late-binding closure wires every registered handler to the last config in the loop, so a retry policy or a route table silently applies one entry's settings to all of them. A closure capturing a large object pins it for the closure's lifetime, and when the closure is stored in a module-level registry that is a leak with no obvious owner — RSS climbs and the profiler points at the captured object rather than at the function holding it. And closures cannot cross a process boundary, so a design that works under threads fails on the day someone swaps in a ProcessPoolExecutor, with a pickling error that names something unrelated.

The business framing is that none of these are visible at definition time, and the first two do not raise at all. Knowing that capture is a live shared cell — not a value copy — is what lets you predict lifetime, memory and the loop bug from reading the code.

Real World Usage

Not a distinguishing product feature, but the mechanism underlies a great deal of library code. functools.partial and every stateful decorator are closures over configuration and the wrapped callable; retry and backoff libraries like tenacity build their wrappers this way; framework route and handler registration captures the handler plus its config; and callback-based APIs throughout asyncio and the GUI toolkits depend on it. The pickling limit is why multiprocessing documentation steers you toward top-level functions, and why task queues require importable callables rather than closures.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — this is a mechanism rather than a performance characteristic, and no defensible citable benchmarks exist. Per the no-fabrication rule, no numbers beat invented ones. The one directional fact worth stating is that LOAD_DEREF is one extra indirection over LOAD_FAST and is not a meaningful hot-path concern.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency Free-variable access is a fast indirection through the cell; negligible against a function call.
💰 Memory Captured cells, and everything reachable from them, stay alive for the closure's lifetime — the real cost, and a genuine leak vector.
🧮 CPU No meaningful cost versus a plain function call.
📈 Scale Closures do not cross process boundaries, which constrains multiprocessing and task-queue designs.
🔧 Maintainability Excellent for one-method state; opaque once the interface grows, since cells have no names in a debugger.
🐍 CPython-specific State lives in cell objects reachable via __closure__, with names in co_freevars / co_cellvars.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Scope and the LEGB rule — the Enclosing scope and nonlocal are the closure machinery; read that first.

  • Names, binding and assignment — closures capture bindings rather than values, which only makes sense once binding does.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • Decorators — the wrapper is a closure over the decorated function and the decorator's arguments.

  • functools.partial and the functools toolkit — freezing arguments eagerly, and picklable when applied to a top-level function.

  • Generators — the other way a function's state outlives a call, with a whole frame rather than cells.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • A class with __call__ — when state needs multiple methods, serialisation, or introspection.

  • functools.partial — when you only need to pre-bind arguments, not maintain mutable state.

  • contextvars — when the "captured" value should vary per task rather than per closure.

🧩 Composes with

  • The shared-default trap — default arguments are evaluated eagerly, which is precisely why i=i fixes late binding.

  • functools.wraps — preserving the wrapped function's identity across the closure that wraps it.

15. Lock it in

First-class = the function can leave the scope that made it.
Closure = it takes the cells with it — shared, live, and read at call time.

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 A closure is a backpack — the same bag, not a photocopy.

The enclosing function packs a bag and hands it to the inner function on the way out. The room gets torn down, but the bag survives because the inner function is still holding it. Hand the same bag to two functions and one of them rummaging changes what the other finds — and if the enclosing function kept editing the bag right up to the last moment, everyone who walked out sees those final edits.

The bag is a cell object with one slot. The room torn down while the bag survives is the frame being discarded while __closure__ keeps the cell alive. Two functions holding one bag is the shared cell, which is both how sibling closures share state and why every callback built in a loop reports the last value.

notes.title: The Arguments Model (/, *, *args, **kwargs)

headings.text: What's the difference between *args and **kwargs, and between * in a signature versus at a call site?
Why would you deliberately make a parameter positional-only (/) or keyword-only (*) in a production API?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Calls & argument passing — Reference: calls

  • Positional-only parameters — PEP 570

  • Keyword-only arguments — PEP 3102

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Python args and kwargs: demystified

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

* and ** mean one thing in a def and the opposite thing at a call site, and the bare * with no name after it is a third thing again. Most people learn the collecting half, meet / in a traceback from a built-in, and never find out that the markers exist to solve an API-design problem rather than a syntax one.

2. What Python normally does

An ordinary signature gives the caller a free choice.

def connect(host, port):
    return host, port

Both of these work, and the function cannot tell them apart:

>>> connect("db", 5432)
('db', 5432)
>>> connect(host="db", port=5432)
('db', 5432)
>>> connect("db", port=5432)
('db', 5432)

That is the default: every parameter is positional-or-keyword. Python fills parameters left to right from whatever was passed positionally, then applies the keyword arguments by name, and a parameter is satisfied either way.

The consequence is easy to miss and it is the whole reason the rest of this note exists: your parameter names are part of your public API. The moment anyone writes connect(host="db"), renaming host to hostname is a breaking change — even though nothing about the function's behaviour changed.

So by default a caller may pass any argument by position or by name, and every parameter name is a promise you have made.

3. What changes

Two markers let you take that choice back, in either direction.

def connect(host, port, /, timeout=30, *, retries=3):
    return host, port, timeout, retries

Everything before / is positional-only; everything after * is keyword-only; what sits between them keeps the old both-ways behaviour.

>>> connect("db", 5432)
('db', 5432, 30, 3)
>>> connect("db", 5432, 10, retries=5)
('db', 5432, 10, 5)

And the two things that used to work now fail, on purpose:

>>> connect(host="db", port=5432)
TypeError: connect() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'host, port'
>>> connect("db", 5432, 10, 5)
TypeError: connect() takes from 2 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

def connect(host, port, /, timeout=30, *, retries=3, **opts)
            └──────┬─────┘  └────┬────┘   └────┬────┘  └──┬──┘
          positional-only   either way    keyword-only   extra
                                                         keywords
          names are PRIVATE  names public  names are     collected
          — rename freely                  the contract   into a dict

The bare * is worth pausing on, because it is not a collector. *args with a name gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple; a bare * gathers nothing at all and exists purely as a marker saying "everything after me must be passed by keyword".

And the same two symbols reverse meaning at a call site. In a def they pack; in a call they unpack:

>>> args, kw = ("db", 5432), {"retries": 5}
>>> connect(*args, **kw)
('db', 5432, 30, 5)

The trade in one sentence: you give up the caller's freedom to choose, and you get back the ability to rename positional-only parameters without breaking anyone, and to force clarity at call sites that would otherwise read as bare booleans.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Two things about that order matter in practice. Positionals are bound before keywords, which is why passing the same parameter both ways gives you TypeError: got multiple values for argument rather than one silently winning. And defaults are consulted last, only for parameters nothing reached — which is the join to the shared-default trap, since those default objects were built once when the def ran, not now.

The parameter layout itself is stored on the code object, so you can read a function's contract without calling it: co_posonlyargcount, co_argcount and co_kwonlyargcount are the three boundaries, and inspect.signature is the readable front end for them.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
def create_user(name, email, /, role="viewer", *, send_email=True, dry_run=False, **extra):
    #           └── positional-only ──┘  └ either ┘  └──── keyword-only ────┘  └ overflow ┘
    return {"name": name, "email": email, "role": role,
            "send_email": send_email, "dry_run": dry_run, **extra}

create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", send_email=False)        # ✅ flags are self-documenting
# create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", False, True)           # ❌ TypeError — and unreadable
# create_user(name="Raje", email="r@x.io")             # ❌ names stay private, rename-safe

payload = {"role": "admin", "send_email": False}
create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", **payload)               # unpacking at the call site

The design choices are the point, not the syntax. name and email are positional-only because they are obvious in context and their names should not become a compatibility promise. send_email and dry_run are keyword-only because they are booleans, and create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", False, True) is unreadable at the call site and silently wrong if the order is ever changed. role sits in the middle because callers legitimately want it either way. This is exactly why so many CPython built-ins — len, dict.get, str.replace — are positional-only.

7. The deeper mental model

A signature is really answering two independent questions about every parameter:

                       may the caller use the NAME?
                            no              yes
                        ┌───────────┬────────────────┐
   may the caller   no  │  (impossible) │  keyword-only  │   *, flag
   use POSITION?        │               │   name IS the  │
                        │               │    contract    │
                        ├───────────────┼────────────────┤
                    yes │ positional-   │ positional-or- │   default
                        │ only          │ keyword        │
                        │ name is       │ name is        │
                        │ private       │ public         │
                        └───────────────┴────────────────┘
                              a, /          a

Python's default puts every parameter in the bottom-right cell, which is the most permissive and therefore the most expensive to change later. / and * are how you move a parameter out of it deliberately — and the choice is an API-versioning decision, not a style one. Anything positional-only can be renamed in a patch release; anything a caller can name is frozen from the moment someone names it.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Full parameter order? pos_only, /, pos_or_kw, *args, kw_only, **kwargs.
What do / and * mark? / — everything before is positional-only. * — everything after is keyword-only.
*/** in a def vs at a call? Pack in the def (collect into tuple/dict); unpack at the call (spread out).

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Keep it to about twenty seconds out loud.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between *args and **kwargs, and between * in a signature versus at a call site?

*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict — in a signature they are the catch-alls that make a function variadic. At a call site the same stars mean the inverse: f(*my_list) spreads an iterable into positional arguments and f(**my_dict) spreads a mapping into keyword arguments. Same symbols, opposite direction — packing in the def, unpacking in the call.

A bare * with no name is a third thing and catches people out. It is a marker rather than a collector: def f(a, *, b) says b and anything after it must be passed by keyword, while accepting no variadic positionals at all. It is how you get keyword-only parameters without inventing an *args you do not want.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Why would you deliberately make a parameter positional-only (/) or keyword-only (*) in a production API?

🎯 Really testing: whether you think about API stability and call-site clarity rather than just reciting syntax.

Positional-only decouples your parameter names from your public contract. If a parameter is positional-only a caller can never write f(x=...), so you are free to rename it in a later release without breaking anyone — which is exactly why so many CPython built-ins are positional-only, and why dict.get can call its parameter whatever it likes. It also lets you use a name like self or list as a parameter without colliding with a key someone might legitimately want to pass through **kwargs.

Keyword-only does the opposite service: it forces the call site to name the argument, which kills the class of bug where someone writes create_user("admin", True, False) and no reader — including the author six months later — can say what those booleans mean. Flags, rarely-used options and anything whose order could plausibly be misremembered are prime candidates. Used together they let an API evolve safely: hide the names you might want to rename, and force clarity on the options that would otherwise be cryptic positionals.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Marker Meaning Caller must use Name is public?
a positional-or-keyword (the default) either ❌ frozen once anyone names it
a, / positional-only position only ✅ private — rename freely
*, a keyword-only keyword only ❌ the name is the contract
*args collect extra positionals → tuple — n/a
**kwargs collect extra keywords → dict — n/a
bare * marker only, collects nothing — n/a

11. What Goes Wrong

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "* and ** mean the same thing in a def and at a call site."

✅ Reality: In a def they pack — collect extra arguments into a tuple and a dict. At a call site they unpack — spread an iterable and a mapping into arguments. Same syntax, opposite direction.

❌ Misconception: "A bare * in a signature accepts variadic positionals."

✅ Reality: A named *args collects positionals; a bare * collects nothing and is purely a marker forcing everything after it to be keyword-only.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

The arguments model gets conflated with the mutable-default trap, and they are adjacent but distinct. This topic governs how values reach parameters; the default trap is about when the default expression was evaluated — once, at def-time. You can know the call model perfectly and still ship the shared-list bug, because they are answering different questions.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't use a mutable default — def f(x=[]) is evaluated once at def-time and shared across every call. Use the None sentinel; this is a different topic wearing the same syntax.

  • Don't absorb known keys into a sprawling **kwargs — it defeats IDE completion, type checking and help(), and pushes every error from the call site into the body. Prefer explicit parameters, or a dataclass / TypedDict when there are many.

  • Don't pass flags positionally — f("admin", True, False) is unreadable and silently wrong if the order ever changes. Make options keyword-only with *.

  • Don't put required parameters after *args expecting them to stay positional — everything after *args becomes keyword-only, which is usually not what was intended.

  • Don't reach for / in a codebase targeting below 3.8 — the syntax is a SyntaxError there, and it is one of the few things in this note that is version-gated.

🔖 Version discipline

Positional-only / syntax is Python 3.8+ (PEP 570), though CPython's own built-ins behaved this way long before the syntax was available to user code. Keyword-only * is 3.0+ (PEP 3102). Def-time default evaluation is stable across all of 3.x. For typing variadic signatures, ParamSpec is 3.10+ and TypeVarTuple / Unpack are 3.11+ — check your floor before relying on either.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Names, binding and assignment — parameters are local bindings created at call time, nothing more.

  • Mutable vs immutable and the shared-default trap — where default-evaluation timing is covered properly.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • Decorators — def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) with return func(*args, **kwargs) is the universal pass-through, and it exists because of this model.

  • functools.partial — pre-binding positional and keyword arguments onto a callable.

  • Type hints — ParamSpec and Concatenate exist to type exactly this model across a decorator boundary.

15. Lock it in

`/` makes names private (rename-safe); `*` makes names required (self-documenting).
In a `def` the stars pack; at a call site they unpack.
