headings.text: What does @functools.wraps actually do, and what breaks if you omit it?
Walk me through exactly what Python does when it evaluates @my_decorator above a def, and explain the order for stacked decorators.
A teammate puts @functools.cache on an instance method to speed it up, and a long-running service slowly leaks memory. What's happening?
Design a decorator-based cross-cutting layer for a service — auth, rate limiting, retries, metrics — that stacks cleanly on your endpoint handlers. Where does the decorator approach break at scale?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Decorator grammar — Reference: function definitions

  • functools.wraps — functools.wraps

  • Relaxed grammar — PEP 614 — relaxing grammatical restrictions on decorators

  • Bonus — Real Python: Primer on Python decorators

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — GeeksforGeeks: Decorators in Python

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

Decorators look like an annotation — a marker you attach to a function to tag it with some behaviour — and that reading is wrong in a way that makes everything afterwards confusing. It leaves you unable to say when the decorator runs, why stacking two of them has an order at all, or why a decorator that takes an argument suddenly needs three nested functions instead of two.

The problem they solve is genuinely important: logging, timing, auth, retries, caching and route registration are all things you need on a hundred functions and do not want written inside any of them.

So hold this question the whole way through: what is @ actually shorthand for? It is one line of desugaring, and every hard question about decorators is answered by applying it literally.

2. What Python normally does

Two facts you already have, put next to each other.

The first is that def is a binding statement. It builds a function object and binds a name to it — no more magical than x = 5:

def greet(name):
    return f"hello {name}"

>>> greet
<function greet at 0x7f9c2d1a4040>

The second is that nothing stops you rebinding that name to something else afterwards, including something built from the original function:

def logged(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print(f"calling {func.__name__}")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

greet = logged(greet)

logged took a function and returned a different function — a closure holding the original in a cell. Then the assignment pointed the name greet at the replacement. Now every caller who says greet(...) reaches the wrapper, and the wrapper reaches the original:

>>> greet("Raje")
calling greet
'hello Raje'

Nobody's call site changed. They still write greet("Raje"), because the name is the only thing they ever had.

BEFORE                          AFTER  greet = logged(greet)

 "greet" ──→ [original fn]       "greet" ──→ [wrapper]
                                                 │ (cell)
                                                 ▼
                                            [original fn]

So the whole capability already exists in plain Python: build a replacement from a function, and rebind the name to it.

3. What changes

Nothing about the mechanism. What changes is where you write it.

@logged
def greet(name):
    return f"hello {name}"

That is exactly greet = logged(greet), executed the instant the def finishes. Same call, same rebinding, same result — moved from three lines below the function to one line above it, where a reader sees it before reading the body.

That relocation is the entire feature, and it is worth being blunt about it because the sugar is what makes people think something else is going on. The decorator is not attached to the function, not consulted per call, and not stored anywhere by the interpreter. It runs once, at definition time, and its return value becomes the function.

Which means this is legal and does what it says:

def deco(func):
    return 42

@deco
def f():
    ...

>>> f
42

Nothing requires a decorator to return a function at all. f is now an integer, because f = deco(f) is all that happened.

But something did break in the useful version, and it is the thing you have to fix in every decorator you ever write:

>>> greet.__name__
'wrapper'
>>> greet.__doc__ is None
True

The name greet now points at the wrapper, and the wrapper is a different object with its own metadata. Tracebacks say wrapper, help() shows the wrong signature, and anything keying off __name__ — API routers, test collectors, serialisers — now sees the wrong function. functools.wraps is the fix, and it is a two-line addition that copies the original's identity onto the replacement:

import functools

def logged(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)          # copies __name__, __doc__, __qualname__,
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):   # __module__, __dict__; sets __wrapped__
        print(f"calling {func.__name__}")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

WITHOUT wraps                    WITH wraps

"greet" ──→ wrapper              "greet" ──→ wrapper
             __name__ 'wrapper'               __name__  'greet'
             __doc__  None                    __doc__   original's
                                              __wrapped__ ──→ original

The trade in one sentence: you get to move cross-cutting behaviour out of every function body and declare it above the signature, and you pay by replacing the function object — so you must carry its identity across by hand.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

The mechanism is grammar, not runtime machinery, so the useful depth here is in what the desugaring implies once there is more than one decorator or an argument involved.

Stacking is just nesting, so the order follows from the desugaring. @a over @b over def f is f = a(b(f)). Read it as an expression and both halves are obvious: b is applied first because it is the inner call, so application is bottom-up; but at call time control enters the outermost wrapper first, so a's pre-code runs before b's and execution is top-down. Saying only one of those two halves is the classic half-learned answer.

A decorator with an argument is a factory, and that is one extra layer rather than an optional parameter. @retry(max_attempts=3) desugars to f = retry(max_attempts=3)(f). The retry(3) call happens first and must return a decorator, which is then called with the function. So the shape is three nested functions — factory, decorator, wrapper — where the plain form has two. Drawing two layers when the decorator takes arguments is one of the most common whiteboard mistakes.

The wrapper's signature is what makes it reusable. def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) plus return func(*args, **kwargs) is the universal pass-through: it forwards everything and returns the result untouched. A wrapper that hard-codes a signature only works for one function, and — far more dangerously — a wrapper that calls func(...) without return silently converts every result to None.

One detail worth knowing because it explains a whole class of async bugs: a decorator has no idea whether the function it wraps is a coroutine function. A sync wrapper applied to an async def returns the coroutine object without awaiting it, so the body never runs and nothing raises at the decoration site. Async cross-cutting layers need async def wrapper with await func(...), and a decorator meant for both has to branch on inspect.iscoroutinefunction(func) at decoration time.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import functools, time

def retry(max_attempts: int = 3, backoff: float = 0.1):
    def decorator(func):                            # ← the actual decorator
        @functools.wraps(func)                      # ✅ carry identity across
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):               # ← closes over func + config
            for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)    # ✅ MUST return, or you get None
                except ConnectionError:
                    if attempt == max_attempts:
                        raise                       # exhausted: let it propagate
                    time.sleep(backoff * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
        return wrapper
    return decorator                                # ← three layers, because of the args

@retry(max_attempts=3)                              # retry(3) → decorator → wrapper
def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    """Fetch a URL."""
    return "ok"

print(fetch.__name__, fetch.__doc__)                # fetch  Fetch a URL.
print(fetch.__wrapped__)                            # <function fetch ...> — the original

Three things in that snippet are the difference between a decorator that survives review and one that does not. @functools.wraps(func) keeps fetch identifiable in tracebacks and to anything reading __name__, and gives you __wrapped__ so inspect.signature can see through the wrapper. The return in front of func(...) is the one-character bug that turns every response into None. And catching ConnectionError specifically rather than Exception is what stops the retry loop from swallowing genuine programming errors and retrying a non-idempotent operation three times.

6. Break it yourself

Paste this in. It puts a print statement in the decorator body itself, which settles the "when does it run" question in a way no amount of explanation does.

def noisy(func):
    print(f"DECORATING {func.__name__}")
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print("  wrapper running")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@noisy
def f():
    return 1

print("--- definition finished, nothing called yet ---")
f()
f()
print(f.__name__)          # ?

# what to look for: DECORATING prints BEFORE the marker line and only once,
#                   while "wrapper running" prints once per call
# naive model would predict: DECORATING appears each time f() is called

You get DECORATING f, then the marker, then wrapper running twice, then wrapper.

Two things are proved at once. The decorator ran during the def, before any call, and exactly once no matter how many times f is invoked — so whatever expensive setup a decorator does is an import-time cost, not a per-request one. And f.__name__ is wrapper, because no functools.wraps was applied; the name f is genuinely bound to a different object now, and that object has its own metadata. Add @functools.wraps(func) above def wrapper and rerun: the last line flips to f while everything else stays identical.

7. The deeper mental model

Zoom out and @ stops being decorator syntax and becomes an instance of something the language does repeatedly:

   @deco                              class-level equivalents
   def f(): ...                       
        ↓                             @property      → f = property(f)
   f = deco(f)                        @staticmethod  → f = staticmethod(f)
        ↓                             @classmethod   → f = classmethod(f)
   "a name is rebound to              @dataclass     → C = dataclass(C)
    something built from              @functools.cache → f = cache(f)
    what the name held"

Every one of those is the same line of desugaring. property, staticmethod and classmethod are not keywords and not compiler features — they are ordinary callables that take a function and return a descriptor, applied by the same f = deco(f) rule. @dataclass takes a class and returns a class with generated methods. There is no separate decorator subsystem to learn.

That works only because of what came before it in this folder. Functions are objects, so they can be passed to and returned from other functions; closures let the returned wrapper keep hold of the original and its configuration; and name binding means replacing a function is just pointing a name somewhere else. Decorators are what you get when you have all three and add one line of grammar.

So the honest one-line summary is not "decorators modify functions". It is that a decorator replaces a function and rebinds its name, once, at definition time — and everything else, including the stacking order and the three-layer factory, follows from reading f = a(b(f)) literally.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does @deco desugar to? f = deco(f) — run once, at def-time, immediately after the def builds the function.
What does @functools.wraps preserve? __name__, __doc__, __qualname__, __module__, __dict__; and sets __wrapped__.
Stacked decorator order? Bottom-up application, top-down execution. @a over @b is a(b(f)).
@deco(arg) — how many layers? Three: factory → decorator → wrapper. It's deco(arg)(f).
The universal wrapper signature? def wrapper(*args, **kwargs) with return func(*args, **kwargs).
Why does @cache on a method leak? The cache key includes self, so it pins every instance for the process lifetime.
Sync decorator on an async def? Returns the coroutine unawaited — the body never runs, and nothing raises.

🖼️ Visual Recall

Include — the wrap-and-replace pipeline is the concept. Re-label the Section 4 Mermaid nodes A–I and reconstruct cold; the answer key is build f0 → apply inner → apply outer → bind the name once → calls enter outermost-first and unwind back.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Said aloud it runs about twenty seconds, which is what you get before the follow-up lands. Everything below Tier 1 is what they follow up with.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What does @functools.wraps actually do, and what breaks if you omit it?

functools.wraps is itself a decorator — a thin wrapper over functools.update_wrapper — that you apply to your inner wrapper function. It copies the wrapped function's identifying metadata onto the replacement: __name__, __qualname__, __doc__, __module__ and __dict__, and it sets __wrapped__ pointing at the original so tools can unwrap the chain.

Omit it and the decorated function reports itself as wrapper. help() shows the wrong name and docstring, tracebacks and log lines name wrapper instead of the real function, inspect.signature reports (*args, **kwargs) instead of the real parameters, and anything keyed off __name__ — API routers, test collectors, some serialisers — misbehaves. It is a two-line fix that a senior includes reflexively, and forgetting it is a well-known interview tell.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Walk me through exactly what Python does when it evaluates @my_decorator above a def, and explain the order for stacked decorators.

🎯 Really testing: whether you know decoration happens at definition time, and whether you can state both halves of the stacking order.

When Python executes the def statement it builds the function object normally, and then — before binding it to its name — applies the decorator: it calls my_decorator(func) and binds the return value to that name in the enclosing namespace. So the decorated form is exactly f = my_decorator(f). This happens once, at definition time, which for a module-level function means at import; the per-call cost afterwards is only whatever the returned wrapper does. Nothing constrains the return value either — if the decorator returns a non-callable, the name is now bound to that non-callable.

For stacking, the rule is bottom-up application and top-down execution, and both halves come from reading the desugaring. @a over @b over def f is f = a(b(f)): b is the inner call so it wraps the raw function first, which is the bottom-up half. At call time, though, control enters the outermost wrapper first, so a's pre-code runs before b's and the result unwinds back out through b then a — the top-down half. The way I keep them straight is that the layers are peeled onto the function from the closest outward, but a call knocks on the outermost door first.

Tier 3 — Failure modes

A teammate puts @functools.cache on an instance method to speed it up, and a long-running service slowly leaks memory. What's happening?

📍 Seen in the wild: the canonical decorator memory bug, and a favourite because it looks like an obvious optimisation.

functools.cache and lru_cache store a mapping from the call's arguments to its result, and for a method the first argument is self. So every distinct instance that ever calls the method becomes part of a cache key, in a cache that lives on the function object — which lives on the class, for the process lifetime. The cache therefore holds a strong reference to every one of those instances forever, preventing collection long after the application has dropped them. In a service creating many short-lived objects that is a textbook slow leak: RSS climbs in proportion to cumulative instance creation rather than to live application state or request rate.

Two things make it worse than it first appears. functools.cache is unbounded entirely, and lru_cache(maxsize=N) is bounded only by entry count, never by instance lifetime — so a bound limits how bad it gets without fixing the cause. And because the cache is on the function, it is shared across every instance rather than being per-instance, which means it is also a correctness risk if the cached value is instance-specific in a way the key does not capture.

The fix depends on the intent. For per-instance memoisation, functools.cached_property stores the value on the instance, so it is collected with the instance. For a genuinely shared cache, key it on the immutable identifying fields rather than on self — pull the computation out into a module-level function taking those fields — and bound it with maxsize plus eviction or a TTL. The monitorable signature is worker RSS tracking cumulative object creation, which distinguishes it from an ordinary capacity problem.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a decorator-based cross-cutting layer for a service — auth, rate limiting, retries, metrics — that stacks cleanly on your endpoint handlers. Where does the decorator approach break at scale?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can compose decorators as a deliberate pipeline, and whether you know where framework middleware takes over.

The binding constraint is ordering, because these decorators compose into an effective request pipeline and the order changes what each one measures and protects. I would fix it deliberately: metrics and tracing outermost, so they time everything including retries and rejections; then auth, so an unauthenticated request is rejected before any work is done; then rate limiting; then retries innermost, closest to the actual call, so a retry does not re-run the auth check or count as three requests in the metrics. Each layer is a wraps-preserving wrapper with a (*args, **kwargs) signature so it stays handler-agnostic, and the configurable ones are factories — @retry(max=3), @rate_limit(rps=10) — where the outer call captures config, the middle layer is the decorator, and the inner wrapper closes over both the config and the handler.

Where it breaks is runtime flexibility. Decorators bind at definition time to one specific function, so the stack cannot be reordered, toggled by config, or applied across a whole route tree without editing every handler. The moment you need per-deployment policy, a kill switch, or something that applies to routes registered by a third-party library, that is ASGI or WSGI middleware, or a dependency-injection system like FastAPI's Depends. The honest framing is that decorators are the right tool for per-handler concerns and the wrong one for app-wide policy, and a mature codebase uses both.

Async is the sharp edge I would raise unprompted. A decorator written for sync functions applied to an async def returns the coroutine without awaiting it, so the handler body never executes and nothing raises at decoration time — the endpoint just returns a coroutine object. Any cross-cutting layer for async handlers needs async def wrappers with await, or a branch on inspect.iscoroutinefunction if it must serve both. Related: a decorator that does blocking I/O inside an async wrapper stalls the entire event loop for every request, which is a far more expensive mistake than the equivalent in a threaded server.

The failure mode I would monitor first is a wrapper silently swallowing results or exceptions — the missing return func(...) that turns every response into None, or a @retry catching Exception broadly and retrying a non-idempotent write. Both are invisible until one specific path exercises them, so I would add a contract test asserting that a decorated handler returns what the undecorated one returns, and alert on handlers returning unexpected None.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Function decorator Class decorator (__call__)
Shape closure returning a wrapper a class whose instances are callable
State lives in closure cells instance attributes (self)
Best for simple wrap-and-forward decorators needing rich, introspectable state
Preserving identity @functools.wraps(func) functools.update_wrapper(self, func) in __init__
Introspection opaque cells named attributes
On methods works naturally needs __get__ care, since it isn't a plain function

Decorators with arguments are orthogonal to this axis — either form becomes a factory by adding one outer layer.

11. What Goes Wrong

Two different failure modes sit under this heading: wrong beliefs about how decoration works, which produce bugs, and delivery mistakes when explaining it, which cost offers.

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A decorator runs every time the function is called."

✅ Reality: The decorator runs once, at definition time — f = deco(f). Only the returned wrapper runs per call. Section 6 makes the difference visible in one paste.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "@deco and @deco(arg) are the same shape, with an optional argument."

✅ Reality: @deco(arg) is a decorator factory — three nested functions, not two. deco(arg) is called first and must return the real decorator, which is then called with the function.

❌ Misconception: "A decorator has to return a function."

✅ Reality: It can return anything; whatever it returns becomes the name's new value. That is exactly how property, staticmethod and classmethod work — they return descriptors, not functions.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

Decorators get conflated with the closures that implement them, and the two are different levels. A decorator is the pattern — a callable that replaces a function and rebinds its name at definition time. A closure is the usual mechanism, since the wrapper generally closes over func. But a decorator need not be a closure: a class with __call__ is one, and functools.lru_cache applied directly is one. Conversely most closures are not decorators. Keep the pattern separate from its common implementation.

Interview Traps

  • Explaining decorators without ever saying functools.wraps — the single most common tell. A senior mentions it unprompted and can list what it preserves.

  • Giving only one half of the stacking order — say both: bottom-up application (a(b(f))), top-down execution (a's pre-code first). Naming one half reads as half-learned.

  • Drawing two layers for @deco(arg) — it is three, and not recognising the factory shape is an immediate signal you have used decorators without writing one.

  • Forgetting *args, **kwargs pass-through — a wrapper that hard-codes a signature only works for one function.

  • Saying the decorator "runs at call time" — it runs at def-time, and conflating them misses the whole point of the desugaring. Say f = deco(f) out loud; it answers most follow-ups by itself.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

When TO use this

  • Cross-cutting concerns that would otherwise be copy-pasted into every function body — logging, timing, auth checks, retries, caching, metrics, transaction and DB-session boundaries.

  • A factory when the behaviour is configurable — @retry(max_attempts=5), @rate_limit(rps=10), @cache(ttl=60) — capturing the configuration in the outer layer so the call site reads as a declaration.

  • functools.wraps in every wrapper you write — non-negotiable, and cheap enough that there is no case for skipping it.

  • A class-based decorator when the wrapper needs rich, introspectable state — call counts, a registry, reconfigurable policy — where named attributes beat opaque cells.

  • Registration — @app.get("/x"), @pytest.fixture, @click.command — where the decorator's job is the side effect of registering, not wrapping at all.

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't write a wrapper without functools.wraps — you break help(), inspect.signature, tracebacks, and anything reading __name__ or __doc__.

  • Don't apply a sync decorator to an async def — it returns the coroutine unawaited and the body never runs, with no error at decoration time. Write an async wrapper that awaits, or branch on inspect.iscoroutinefunction.

  • Don't put @cache or @lru_cache on an instance method — the key includes self and pins every instance for the process lifetime. Use cached_property, or key on immutable fields with a bound.

  • Don't reach for a decorator when you need runtime-configurable ordering or app-wide policy — decorators bind at def-time to one function. That is what ASGI/WSGI middleware and dependency injection are for.

  • Don't forget to return func(...) — a wrapper that calls the function without returning its result silently makes every response None, and no test that only checks for absence of exceptions will catch it.

  • Don't stack decorators deeply on a hot path without looking — each layer adds a call frame per request and obscures the traceback, which costs more in debugging time than in latency.

🔖 Version discipline

Decorator syntax and functools.wraps are stable across all of Python 3.x. PEP 614 (3.9+) relaxed the grammar so that any expression can be a decorator rather than only a dotted name with an optional call — older material describing that restriction is out of date. functools.cache is 3.9+ and is equivalent to lru_cache(maxsize=None). functools.cached_property is 3.8+, and its behaviour around locking changed in 3.12, so check the version before relying on its thread-safety characteristics. For typing decorators without destroying the wrapped signature, ParamSpec and Concatenate are 3.10+ (or via typing_extensions below that).

13. Production Reality

Decorators are how Python expresses cross-cutting concerns, which means a subtle bug in one is amortised across the entire request volume of a service.

Why It Matters in Production

Get them right and one @retry or @traced cleanly covers hundreds of call sites with a change reviewable in one place. Get them wrong and the failures are systemic rather than local. A wrapper missing functools.wraps breaks every traceback and every API route that reads __name__, so the first incident where you need a clean stack trace is the one where you do not get one. A wrapper missing its return turns every response into None on whichever paths use it. A caching decorator on a method OOMKills a worker overnight. A sync decorator on an async handler stops the handler body from ever executing.

The business framing is that decoration happens once at import while the wrapper runs on every single call, so the blast radius of a decorator bug is the full traffic of every function it is applied to — and because the decorator is written once and applied widely, code review attention is concentrated in exactly the wrong place.

Real World Usage

Decorator-first APIs are everywhere in the ecosystem. FastAPI and Flask register routes with @app.get(...); pytest drives collection and parameterisation through @pytest.fixture and @pytest.mark.parametrize; tenacity provides @retry as a production-grade version of the Section 5 example; click builds entire CLIs from @click.command. Inside the standard library, dataclasses.dataclass, functools.lru_cache, property, classmethod, staticmethod, contextlib.contextmanager and functools.singledispatch are all decorators, which is the strongest evidence that the pattern is a language-level idiom rather than a framework trick. Django's @login_required remains the canonical cross-cutting auth example.

Key Numbers & Trade-offs

Skipped — a decorator's cost is entirely whatever the wrapper does, so there is nothing generalisable to cite, and per the no-fabrication rule no numbers beat invented ones. The one directional fact is that each layer adds one call frame per invocation, which is negligible outside pathologically deep stacks.

Dimension Trade-off
⚡ Latency One extra call frame per layer per call — negligible unless stacked deeply on a hot path.
💰 Memory Wrappers hold closure cells containing the wrapped function and its config; caching decorators can grow without bound.
🧮 CPU Whatever the wrapper does. The decoration itself is a one-time import-time cost.
📈 Scale Def-time binding means no runtime reordering or toggling — middleware and DI win for app-wide policy.
🔧 Maintainability DRY for cross-cutting concerns, but deep stacks obscure tracebacks and control flow, and hide where behaviour comes from.
🐍 CPython-specific @ inserts f = deco(f) at def-time; functools.wraps sets __wrapped__, which inspect.unwrap and inspect.signature follow.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • First-class functions and closures — the wrapper is a closure over the decorated function, and this is the mechanism doing the work.

  • Scope and the LEGB rule — decorator factories depend on enclosing-scope capture of the configuration.

  • Names, binding and assignment — @deco is a rebinding, and reading it that way answers most questions.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • The functools toolkit — wraps, lru_cache / cache, partial, cached_property, singledispatch.

  • Descriptors — property, classmethod and staticmethod are decorator-built descriptors.

  • Metaclasses and __init_subclass__ — class decoration as the lighter-weight alternative to a metaclass.

  • Async functions — where the sync-wrapper trap lives, and why async needs its own wrapper shape.

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • ASGI/WSGI middleware and dependency injection (FastAPI Depends) — when policy must be app-wide or configurable at runtime.

  • Plain higher-order functions — when the @ sugar is not worth the indirection, or when the wrapping is conditional.

  • Context managers — when the concern is a block of code rather than a whole function.

🧩 Composes with

  • functools.wraps — the mandatory partner inside every wrapper.

  • ParamSpec and Concatenate — typing a decorator so the wrapped signature survives for type checkers.

  • inspect.iscoroutinefunction — branching a decorator so it serves both sync and async targets.

15. Lock it in

`@deco` is `f = deco(f)` — once, at definition time, rebinding the name.
Application is bottom-up; execution is top-down; `@deco(arg)` adds a third layer.

⚠️ The symmetry above is the thing to memorise. The hook below is optional and does a different job.

🪝 Optional: a story hook

🪝 Wrap, replace, preserve.

At definition time you hand your function to the decorator. It slips the function inside a wrapper, hangs that wrapper on the original name so every caller now reaches the wrapper first, and copies the original's nameplate and docstring across so it still answers to its own name. Stack two and they are peeled on from the inside out — but a knock at the door reaches the outermost one first.

Wrap is the closure capturing func. Replace is f = deco(f) rebinding the name to the wrapper. Preserve is functools.wraps copying __name__, __doc__ and setting __wrapped__. And the knock at the door is why application is bottom-up while execution is top-down.

notes.title: The functools Toolkit (lru_cache, partial, singledispatch, cached_property, reduce)

headings.text: What's the difference between functools.partial and a lambda that does the same thing?
Why does @lru_cache on an instance method leak memory, and what should you use instead?

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The module — functools — higher-order functions

  • lru_cache / cache — functools.lru_cache

  • cached_property — functools.cached_property

  • singledispatch — functools.singledispatch

  • 📖 Plain-English walkthrough — Real Python: Caching in Python with lru_cache

🧭 UNDERSTAND BLOCK (Sections 1–7)

1. Why this trips people up

functools reads like a grab-bag of unrelated conveniences, so most people learn lru_cache as "the fast decorator" and stop. That framing is the problem: it hides the fact that lru_cache is a cache with every hazard a cache has, and that half the module exists specifically to give you a safer version of something you would otherwise hand-roll.

2. What Python normally does

Every tool in this module replaces something you can already write by hand, and seeing the hand-rolled version is what makes the trade visible.

Memoisation is a dict you check before computing:

_memo = {}

def slow(n):
    if n not in _memo:
        _memo[n] = n ** 2          # pretend this is expensive
    return _memo[n]

Pre-binding an argument is a lambda:

double = lambda x: x * 2

And branching on a type is a chain of isinstance checks:

def describe(x):
    if isinstance(x, int):
        return f"int: {x}"
    elif isinstance(x, list):
        return f"list of {len(x)}"
    return f"generic: {x!r}"

All three work. All three also have the same quiet defect: _memo grows forever and nobody will notice, the lambda is opaque to every tool that tries to inspect it, and the isinstance chain has to be edited in one central place every time a new type appears.

So the baseline is that you can build all of this yourself, and the hand-rolled versions are unbounded, uninspectable and closed to extension.

3. What changes

functools gives you the same three things with those defects addressed — and, in the case of caching, a new and sharper one.

import functools, operator

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)      # bounded, and it reports on itself
def slow(n):
    return n ** 2

double = functools.partial(operator.mul, 2)     # inspectable and picklable

@functools.singledispatch                        # open to extension
def describe(x):
    return f"generic: {x!r}"

@describe.register
def _(x: int):
    return f"int: {x}"

What you gain is concrete. The cache has a bound and tells you whether it is earning its keep:

>>> slow(4); slow(4)
>>> slow.cache_info()
CacheInfo(hits=1, misses=1, maxsize=128, currsize=1)

The partial can be examined, and — unlike a lambda — sent to another process:

>>> double.func, double.args
(<built-in function mul>, (2,))

And singledispatch moves the type branching out of the function, so a new type registers its own handler from anywhere, including a module the original author never saw.

What you lose is the part people miss. lru_cache puts its memo table on the function object, which lives for the life of the process, and it requires the arguments to be hashable:

>>> slow([1, 2])
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

HAND-ROLLED MEMO                 @lru_cache

_memo = {}                       cache lives on the function object
  ↓ module-level dict              ↓ same lifetime — the whole process
  grows forever                    bounded by maxsize (by COUNT, not bytes)
  any key you like                 keys must be hashable
  you can clear it                 .cache_clear() / .cache_info()

The trade in one sentence: you get bounded, inspectable, extensible versions of things you would otherwise hand-roll — and in exchange the cache becomes process-lifetime shared state living somewhere you did not put it.

4. How It Works (Mechanism, CPython Internals or Runtime Behavior)

Two details in that flow explain most of the module's sharp edges.

The cache is keyed on all the arguments, and it lives on the function. On a plain function that is fine. On an instance method the first argument is self, so every instance that ever calls the method becomes part of a key in a table attached to the class — and held by a strong reference, for the process lifetime. That is the leak, and it is a direct consequence of where the table lives rather than a bug.

maxsize bounds entry count, not memory. A hundred and twenty-eight cached entries could be a hundred and twenty-eight integers or a hundred and twenty-eight DataFrames, and lru_cache cannot tell the difference. It is a bound, not a budget.

cached_property sidesteps both by being a non-data descriptor, which is worth knowing because it explains the behaviour exactly. On first access the descriptor runs and writes its result straight into the instance's __dict__ under the same name. An instance dictionary shadows a non-data descriptor, so every later access finds the stored value and never reaches the descriptor at all — the cache is per instance, collected with the instance, and free on subsequent reads.

5. Code / Config Example

# production-style, not tutorial-style
# this code's mechanism is walked through in Section 4
import functools, operator

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1024)          # ✅ ALWAYS bound it; check cache_info()
def resolve_tenant(tenant_id: str) -> dict: # hashable args, deterministic, no I/O side effects
    return {"id": tenant_id}

double = functools.partial(operator.mul, 2) # picklable → safe for a ProcessPoolExecutor,
                                            # which a lambda is not

@functools.singledispatch                   # dispatches on the FIRST argument's type
def render(value) -> str:
    return str(value)

@render.register                            # new types register from anywhere —
def _(value: list) -> str:                  # no central if/elif to edit
    return ", ".join(render(v) for v in value)

class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows

    @functools.cached_property              # ✅ per-instance memo; dies with the instance.
    def stats(self) -> dict:                #    @lru_cache here would pin every Dataset
        return {"n": len(self.rows)}        #    for the process lifetime

The comments carry the decisions, because this is a toolkit note and the surrounding prose is what gets skipped on a re-read. maxsize is present because the unbounded form is a leak waiting for enough distinct inputs. partial is chosen over a lambda specifically for the process-pool boundary. And cached_property is on stats rather than lru_cache because the correct scope for that cache is one object, not the whole process — which is the single most useful distinction in the module.

7. The deeper mental model

Every tool here is the same move: take a pattern you would write inline and give it a named scope and lifetime.

   hand-rolled                     functools                 what was really fixed

   module-level memo dict     →    @lru_cache(maxsize)       a bound, and introspection
   memo dict on self          →    @cached_property          lifetime tied to the instance
   lambda closing over a val  →    partial(f, val)           inspectable, picklable
   if/elif isinstance chain   →    @singledispatch           extension point, not a chain
   accumulator loop           →    reduce(op, xs)            (rarely an improvement)

Read down the right-hand column and the question every one of them answers is who owns this state, and when does it die? A module-level dict has no answer, which is why it leaks. lru_cache answers "the function, bounded by count". cached_property answers "the instance". A partial answers "the object you were handed, and you can look inside it".

That is also why reduce is the odd one out and is used far less than the rest. It does not change any lifetime or ownership — it just spells a loop differently — which is why sum, math.prod, str.join and any/all beat it almost every time.

📘 REFERENCE BLOCK (Sections 8–15)

8. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two lru_cache traps? Process-lifetime memory (pins self on methods); arguments must be hashable.
partial vs a lambda? partial exposes .func / .args / .keywords and is picklable over top-level functions.
cached_property vs lru_cache on a method? Stored in the instance __dict__, so it dies with the instance — no global pinning.

9. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

🗣️ Tier 1 is the spoken answer. Keep it to about twenty seconds out loud.

Tier 1 — Verifier

What's the difference between functools.partial and a lambda that does the same thing?

Both pre-bind arguments — partial(f, 2) and lambda x: f(2, x) fix the same first argument. The differences are introspection and serialisation. A partial object exposes .func, .args and .keywords, so debuggers, logs and tooling can see exactly what it wraps and what has been bound; a lambda is an opaque <lambda> with none of that.

The one that actually decides designs is pickling. A partial over a top-level function is picklable, so it can cross a multiprocessing or ProcessPoolExecutor boundary or go into a task queue — a lambda cannot be pickled at all. For a throwaway local one-liner a lambda is fine; for anything that will be inspected, logged, or sent to another process, partial is the correct tool.

Tier 2 — Mechanism

Why does @lru_cache on an instance method leak memory, and what should you use instead?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know where the cache physically lives and what reference semantics that implies.

lru_cache stores its memo table on the function object, which is a class attribute shared by every instance and alive for the whole process. Decorating an instance method means the cache key includes self, so every distinct instance that ever calls the method becomes part of a key — and the table holds a strong reference to it. That instance can then never be collected while the cache lives, so in a long-running service that churns through objects, RSS grows with cumulative instance count rather than with live state or request rate. Bounding it with maxsize limits how bad it gets without addressing the cause, and functools.cache is unbounded entirely.

The right tool for per-instance memoisation is cached_property, for the zero-argument, property-shaped case. It works by being a non-data descriptor: on first access it computes the value and writes it into the instance's own __dict__ under the same name, and because an instance dict shadows a non-data descriptor, every later access reads the stored value and never reaches the descriptor. The cache therefore lives on the instance and is collected with it. If you need a parameterised per-instance cache, use an explicit dict on the instance; if you genuinely want a shared one, pull the computation out to a module-level function keyed on the immutable identifying fields rather than on self, and bound it.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Tool What it does Where the state lives Key trap
lru_cache / cache memoise by arguments on the function — process lifetime unbounded without maxsize; needs hashable args; pins self on methods
cached_property memoise a zero-arg property in the instance __dict__ not thread-safe on first compute
partial pre-bind arguments in the partial object pre-bound keywords can still be overridden by the caller
singledispatch type-based overloading in a registry on the function dispatches on the first argument only
wraps preserve wrapped metadata on the wrapper belongs in every decorator you write
reduce fold an iterable to a scalar — usually less readable than sum / math.prod / a loop

11. What Goes Wrong

Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "lru_cache is a free speedup you can put on anything."

✅ Reality: It is process-lifetime shared state with every hazard a cache has. Without maxsize it grows without bound, it requires hashable arguments, and on a method it pins every instance.

❌ Misconception: "functools.partial is just a lambda with nicer syntax."

✅ Reality: A partial is introspectable via .func / .args / .keywords and picklable over top-level functions, so it survives a process boundary. A lambda is opaque and unpicklable.

🔀 Orthogonality callout

lru_cache on a method and cached_property look interchangeable and differ in the thing that matters: where the cache lives. lru_cache stores globally on the function and keys on self, which pins the instance; cached_property stores in the instance __dict__, so it is collected with the object. For per-instance, zero-argument memoisation, cached_property is almost always right.

12. When To Use It — And When Not To

⚠️ When NOT to use this

  • Don't use lru_cache without maxsize on high-cardinality inputs — it grows for the process lifetime until the worker is OOMKilled. Bound it, or use a real cache with eviction and a TTL.

  • Don't put lru_cache on an instance method — it pins every self. Use cached_property, or key a module-level cache on immutable identifying fields.

  • Don't cache a function with unhashable arguments — lists, dicts and sets raise TypeError. Convert to a tuple or frozenset key, or do not cache.

  • Don't cache anything non-deterministic or side-effecting — memoising a call that reads a clock, hits a database, or mutates state returns stale or wrong results silently, which is worse than being slow.

  • Don't assume cached_property is thread-safe on first compute — two threads racing the first access can both compute it. Guard with a lock if the computation is expensive or has side effects.

  • Don't reach for reduce when a built-in exists — sum, math.prod, str.join, any and all are clearer and faster. reduce earns its place only for a genuinely custom fold.

🔖 Version discipline

functools.cache (an alias for lru_cache(maxsize=None)) is 3.9+; cached_property is 3.8+; singledispatch registration by type annotation is 3.7+, and singledispatchmethod is 3.8+. The bare @lru_cache form without parentheses is 3.8+. cached_property dropped its internal per-instance lock in 3.12 — earlier versions serialised first access across all instances, which was a documented performance problem, so its thread-safety characteristics genuinely differ by version and should be checked rather than assumed. Registering singledispatch handlers for union types (int | str) is 3.11+.

14. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites

  • Decorators — every tool here is applied as a decorator or a wrapper, and wraps is part of the module.

  • First-class functions and closures — partial and the cache wrappers close over the target callable.

  • The __eq__ / __hash__ contract — lru_cache keys are dict keys, so everything from that note applies to them.

⬇️ Builds toward

  • Descriptors — cached_property is a non-data descriptor, and the instance-dict shadowing rule is what makes it work.

  • multiprocessing — partial over a top-level function is the picklable way to hand a configured callable to a process pool.

  • Memory diagnosis and weakref — bounding caches, and avoiding the lru_cache-pins-self leak.

15. Lock it in

Every functools tool gives a hand-rolled pattern a named owner and a lifetime.
`lru_cache` lives on the function (process lifetime); `cached_property` lives on the instance.
